claims.claim: Hong Kong should not impose a hard cap on initial rents in subdivided units.
A narrow tightening with stronger tenure security and a light, indexed rent band is the better policy path.
A binding first-generation cap would shrink the stock of subdivided units that the poorest tenants depend on.
SDU tenants pay a 15–25 percent per-square-foot premium over mainstream flats.
Real rent burden for SDU tenants has worsened from 31 to 34 percent.
A 15 percent rent cut would transfer roughly HK$900 per month to incumbent tenants.
A hard cap would prevent 3,000–4,000 households per year from entering the SDU segment, mostly new arrivals and newly formed households.
The long-run supply elasticity for marginal stock is 0.31–0.48, meaning a 10 percent cap-induced rent cut removes 3–5 percent of stock over five years.
The welfare effects of a hard cap are regressive at the entry margin: incumbents gain while outsiders lose.
The 2021 ordinance was a second-generation rent control that capped increases within tenancies but left initial rents untouched.
Academic literature finds second-generation rent controls have small or null effects on stock, while first-generation hard caps cause consistent contraction.
Berlin's 2020 Mietendeckel capped initial offers, leading to a contraction in listings within a year.
When Berlin's rent cap was struck down, suppressed rent increases released and new-contract rents jumped above the pre-cap trend.
Current inspection covers under 6 percent of SDU stock per year, and a band-based cap would require a certifiable tenancy register costing 40–60 staff-years.
Enforcement of a rent cap would systematically miss the most exploited tenants, such as those without written agreements.
In an NGO survey, 61 percent of tenants would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year tenure security, and 74 percent for a faster public-housing offer.
The binding constraint for SDU tenants is the length of the public-housing queue, not rent price.
Landlords are committed to exiting the SDU market if rents fall below mortgage cost.
A hard cap framed as deprivation invites compensation claims and judicial review that would outlast a Council term.
The proportionate policy is tenure security plus an indexed per-square-foot band on initial rents, paired with certification infrastructure.

The strongest argument for a hard cap is distributive: SDU tenants pay a 15–25 percent per-square-foot premium over mainstream flats [D1p1], and real rent burden has worsened from 31 to 34 percent [D2p2].
A cap would transfer real money to incumbents—roughly HK$900 per month under the modelled 15 percent cut [D6p4].
That is not trivial; for Mr Chan it is "food for a month" [D3p2].

But the same model prices the cost: 3,000–4,000 households per year would be unable to enter the segment, "mostly new arrivals and newly formed households" [D6p4]—precisely the population the policy intends to help [D1p2].

But the same model prices the cost: 3,000–4,000 households per year would be unable to enter the segment, "mostly new arrivals and newly formed households" [D6p4]—precisely the population the policy intends to help [D1p2].
The reviewed literature puts long-run supply elasticity for marginal stock at 0.31–0.48, meaning a 10 percent cap-induced rent cut removes 3–5 percent of stock over five years [D6p1].
The welfare arithmetic is therefore regressive at the entry margin: incumbents gain, outsiders lose [D6p3].
The counterargument—that the stable stock under the 2021 ordinance proves regulation is safe [D2p1]—rests on a category error.

The 2021 instrument was second-generation: it capped increases within tenancies but left initial rents untouched [D1p3], and the academic literature finds second-generation controls show "small or null effects on stock," while first-generation hard caps show "consistent contraction effects" [D6p2].

The visible stability is an artifact of a non-binding instrument, exactly as one think-tank piece warns [D12p2].

The lesson is structural, not legal: "the tenants the cap protects are those already inside, and the bill is handed to those still outside" [D7p3].
Current inspection covers under 6 percent of stock per year, and a band-based cap would require a certifiable tenancy register costing 40–60 staff-years [D10p1].

More damning, the tenants least able to complain are those with no written agreement—like Mrs Wong, who has never had one and says the ordinance "changed nothing she can see" [D4p1]—or the newest arrivals.

Enforcement would "systematically miss the most exploited tail" [D10p2], and the subcommittee could not identify any design under which the newest-arrival tail is protected first rather than last [D10p3].

He names the waiting list" [D3p3].

The binding constraint is queue length, not price: the segment is tight because the queue is long, and every enforcement dollar spent policing rents is a dollar not spent on fire, partition and ventilation harms that are "documented and immediate" [D11p2].

The proportionate answer is the middle instrument counsel describes: tenure security plus an indexed per-square-foot band on initial rents, defensible as rate-capping rather than confiscation [D9p2], paired with the certification infrastructure the band requires [D10p1].
